questions.prompt: What is an Apex "callout"?
options: Apex code reaching outside the Salesforce org to talk to another system over the network
A SOQL query that joins two unrelated objects
A trigger that fires before a record is deleted
A Visualforce page's controller constructor
A permission set assignment granted to a user
A Lightning Web Component's wire adapter
questions.explain: A callout is Apex making an outbound HTTP or SOAP request to a system outside Salesforce, and waiting within limits for a response.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes a trigger, not a callout — triggers react to DML events inside the org, while a callout is specifically about reaching an external system over the network. A trigger never, by itself, makes a network request.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a single Apex transaction can make a maximum of ________ callouts to an HTTP request or API call.
questions.explain: The Apex Developer Guide's execution governors and limits reference caps a single transaction at 100 HTTP/API callouts.

questions.prompt: A developer writes Apex that inserts a new Order record and then, in the same transaction, immediately calls out to notify an external warehouse system. What happens when this code runs?
options: It throws a runtime error, because a callout can't be made while there is pending uncommitted DML in the same transaction
It succeeds normally, since callouts and DML can always share a transaction
The DML is silently skipped so the callout can proceed
The callout is automatically deferred to a future transaction with no code change needed
questions.explain: The transaction-ordering rule blocks a callout from running while DML (or other async work or email) is still pending in that same transaction — the callout must come first, or the DML must be moved to a separate async transaction.

questions.prompt: Match each Apex HTTP callout class to what it actually does.
right: The interface implemented to supply a fake response during Apex tests
Builds the outgoing request's endpoint, method, headers, and body
Reads the result of a callout: status code, headers, and body
Performs the callout via its send() method, returning the response
questions.explain: HttpRequest builds the outgoing request, Http.send() performs the callout, HttpResponse holds the result, and HttpCalloutMock is implemented only to fake a response during tests.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between what an External Credential stores and what a Named Credential stores?
options: An External Credential defines the authentication protocol and Principals holding the real auth parameters; a Named Credential defines the endpoint URL and references the External Credential
They store identical information and exist only for naming convenience
A Named Credential stores the password directly, while an External Credential stores only the URL
An External Credential is used only for SOAP callouts, never HTTP
questions.explain: The modern model splits authentication (External Credential, with its Principals) from the endpoint and reference to that authentication (Named Credential) — the Named Credential never stores the password itself.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the default timeout for an Apex HTTP callout, if setTimeout() is never called, is ________ seconds.
questions.explain: The default per-callout timeout is 10 seconds; it can be customized between 1 millisecond and 120,000 milliseconds (120 seconds).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about testing Apex callouts.
options: Apex tests never make real callouts, even if the code under test is identical to production code
A class implementing HttpCalloutMock must provide a respond(HttpRequest req) method
Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mockInstance) registers the mock so real callouts are intercepted for the rest of that test
StaticResourceCalloutMock requires writing a custom class that implements HttpCalloutMock from scratch
If the callout code lives in a managed package, Test.setMock must be called from a test in that same package and namespace
questions.explain: Real callouts are always blocked in test context. HttpCalloutMock requires exactly one method, respond(). Test.setMock registers the mock for interception. StaticResourceCalloutMock is a built-in alternative that does NOT require hand-writing a custom mock class — that statement is false. For managed packages, Test.setMock must be called from within the same package/namespace.

questions.prompt: A callout completes with no CalloutException thrown, but the remote system actually returned a 500 status in its response. What mistake does this scenario illustrate if the code doesn't catch it?
options: Treating the absence of a thrown exception as proof the callout succeeded, instead of checking HttpResponse.getStatusCode()
Calling JSON.serialize() instead of JSON.deserializeUntyped()
Using a Named Credential instead of a literal URL
Setting a timeout above the 120-second maximum
questions.explain: A callout can complete at the HTTP level with no exception while the remote system still reports a failure via its status code — that status must be checked explicitly, since CalloutException only covers connection-level failures.

questions.prompt: What does the @RestResource annotation do in Apex?
options: Exposes an Apex class as a custom REST endpoint, reachable under /services/apexrest/
Publishes an Apex method as a custom SOAP operation
Registers a class as an HttpCalloutMock for testing
Schedules a class to run on a recurring cron-like timer
Marks a method so it can be called from a Platform Event trigger
Grants a Permission Set access to a Named Credential's Principal
questions.explain: @RestResource(urlMapping='/path/*'), applied to a global class, exposes it as a custom REST endpoint under the Apex REST base path.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the webservice keyword, which publishes a SOAP operation, not @RestResource, which is specifically for REST. The two are separate mechanisms covered in different lessons — Apex REST (Lesson 8) and Apex SOAP (Lesson 12).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: each Apex REST HTTP-verb annotation, such as @HttpGet or @HttpPost, can be used only ________ per class.
questions.explain: Each HTTP-verb annotation (@HttpGet, @HttpPost, @HttpPut, @HttpPatch, @HttpDelete) can be used only once per Apex class — one method per verb, per class.

questions.prompt: Why does versioning matter more deliberately for an inbound Apex REST service than for Salesforce's own outbound callout code?
options: Because inbound Apex REST is the contract itself — once an external system has integrated against it, changing it without warning breaks their integration, unlike outbound code which adapts to someone else's existing contract
Because inbound services are not subject to governor limits
Because outbound callouts never need to change over time
Because Apex REST does not support JSON
questions.explain: Inbound integration flips who owns the contract: Salesforce (as the service builder) defines it, so breaking it silently is the developer's own fault, unlike outbound integration where Salesforce is adapting to an external contract it doesn't control.

questions.prompt: Match each inbound authentication concept to what it actually does.
right: Determines what the authenticated call is actually allowed to read or write — authorization, separate from authentication
Defines OAuth scopes, callback URL, and certificate for an external application calling in
Certificate-based flow using a signed token, with no client secret transmitted per request
App authenticates as itself with a client ID and secret, no interactive login
questions.explain: A Connected App is the foundation defining scopes and certificate; Client Credentials authenticates the app itself with a secret; JWT Bearer uses a signed token instead of a transmitted secret; and the integration user's own permissions are the separate authorization check on what an authenticated call can do.

questions.prompt: A team needs to ship a breaking change to an existing Apex REST service's response shape without disrupting callers already integrated against it. What is the most common real-world pattern for this?
options: Encode the version in the urlMapping (e.g. /v1/Accounts/* vs /v2/Accounts/*), usually as a separate class, so existing callers keep working against the old version untouched
Edit the existing method's return type in place and notify callers by email after deploying
Delete the old class immediately so there is only ever one version live
Rely on Salesforce to automatically version every custom Apex REST class
questions.explain: URL-path versioning keeps the old and new versions fully isolated — because each HTTP-verb annotation can only be used once per class, a breaking change typically means a new class with a new mapping rather than editing the old one in place.

questions.prompt: What two requirements must be satisfied for the webservice keyword to successfully expose an Apex method as a SOAP operation?
options: The method must be static, and the containing class must be declared global
The method must be private, and the class must be declared public
The method must implement Queueable, and the class must be abstract
The method must be annotated @HttpPost, and the class must use @RestResource
questions.explain: A webservice method must be static, and its containing class must be global — the keyword cannot be applied to classes, interfaces, interface members, or triggers directly.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about choosing between the standard REST API and a custom Apex REST service for an inbound requirement.
options: The standard REST API already handles plain CRUD on any standard or custom object with no custom code
A custom Apex REST service earns its complexity when the requirement needs logic beyond plain CRUD, such as validation or a multi-object transaction
Custom Apex REST should always be preferred over the standard API, regardless of the requirement
An inbound requirement that is really just "create an Account and some Contacts" is a good candidate for the standard API rather than custom code
The standard REST API cannot be used for SOAP-only external systems
questions.explain: The standard API covers plain CRUD with no code and is the right default; custom Apex REST is justified specifically when logic goes beyond CRUD — always preferring custom Apex regardless of the requirement is the opposite of the lesson's advice. The standard REST API is JSON/REST-based, not a fit for a SOAP-only caller.

questions.prompt: A trigger needs to call out to validate a new Contact's email and later chain a follow-up step depending on the result. Which asynchronous Apex mechanism fits best, and why?
options: Queueable Apex, since it can hold arbitrary state (including SObjects) and one job can enqueue another to chain a sequence of steps
@future(callout=true), since future methods can accept SObject parameters directly
Batch Apex, since it is designed for a single record's validation
Scheduled Apex, since it is the only mechanism that supports callouts
questions.explain: Queueable Apex is a real object that can carry state and chain into further async work, unlike @future methods, which are limited to primitive parameters and cannot chain.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: under the Publish Immediately behavior, EventBus.publish() calls count against a separate, dedicated limit of ________ calls per transaction.
questions.explain: Publish Immediately calls count against a dedicated 150-call-per-transaction limit, checkable with Limits.getPublishImmediateDML(), distinct from the regular DML statement limit that Publish After Commit counts against.

questions.prompt: A developer calls EventBus.publish(evt) and moves on without checking the return value. What risk does this create?
options: None — EventBus.publish() always throws an exception on failure, so an uncaught error would halt the transaction visibly
The event could silently fail to publish, since EventBus.publish() does not throw for an unsuccessful publish — the Database.SaveResult must be checked with isSuccess()/getErrors()
The transaction will always roll back automatically
The platform event definition will be deleted
questions.explain: EventBus.publish() does not throw an exception for a failed publish; code that doesn't inspect the returned SaveResult can silently lose events with no error anywhere in the debug log.

questions.prompt: Match each Change Data Capture changeType value to what triggers it.
right: Lists the specific fields that actually changed; empty on a CREATE
A new tracked record is inserted
An existing tracked record's fields are modified
questions.explain: CREATE fires on insert, UPDATE on a field change, DELETE on removal, and changedFields specifically lists which fields changed on an UPDATE — it stays empty for a CREATE since there's no prior version to compare against.

questions.prompt: What is the central format difference between legacy Outbound Messaging and the modern Flow HTTP Callout action?
options: Outbound Messaging sends SOAP/XML; Flow HTTP Callouts support JSON only
Outbound Messaging requires a Named Credential; Flow HTTP Callouts never use one
Outbound Messaging is triggered by Platform Events; Flow HTTP Callouts are triggered by Workflow Rules
There is no real difference between the two mechanisms
questions.explain: Outbound Messaging is built entirely around SOAP/XML notifications with a required Ack envelope, while Flow HTTP Callouts support only JSON request and response bodies.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of registering a third-party API as an External Service in the correct order.
items: Create a Named Credential pointing at the third-party API's endpoint and authentication
Open the External Services wizard in Setup and select that Named Credential
Import the API's OpenAPI (OAS) specification into the wizard
Salesforce validates the schema, reaches the endpoint, and generates stub Apex classes and invocable actions
questions.explain: Registration starts with the Named Credential (endpoint and auth) already in place, then the wizard is opened and pointed at that credential, the OpenAPI spec is imported, and only then does Salesforce validate and generate the stub classes and invocable actions.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the difference between custom Platform Events and Change Data Capture.
options: A custom Platform Event requires an explicit EventBus.publish() call somewhere in Apex to be published
Change Data Capture publishes automatically whenever a tracked object's records are created, updated, deleted, or undeleted, with no explicit publish call
Both mechanisms use the same underlying Pub/Sub API concept for external subscribers
A custom Platform Event's Publish Behavior setting (Publish After Commit vs Publish Immediately) also applies to Change Data Capture events
In-platform subscribers for both consume events via an Apex trigger on the generated event object
questions.explain: Custom Platform Events require an explicit publish call; CDC publishes automatically once enabled on an object. Both expose a Pub/Sub API channel and support an in-platform Apex trigger subscriber. The Publish Behavior setting is specific to custom Platform Events and does not apply to CDC's automatic publishing.

questions.prompt: A requirement states: "notify the warehouse system that an order was placed, but Salesforce doesn't need to wait for its response." Which named integration pattern does this match?
options: Remote Call-In
Remote Process Invocation – Fire and Forget
Batch Data Synchronization
UI Update Based on Data Changes
questions.explain: Fire and Forget is specifically the pattern where Salesforce calls out to kick off remote work but doesn't wait for it to finish, which matches the "doesn't need to wait for its response" wording exactly.

questions.prompt: Match each integration pattern to the Salesforce mechanism most commonly used to implement it.
left: UI Update Based on Data Changes
right: Platform Events or Change Data Capture driving a live component
Custom Apex REST or the standard REST/SOAP API
A synchronous Apex HTTP callout or Flow HTTP Callout made before dependent DML
Batch Apex kicked off by Scheduled Apex
questions.explain: Remote Call-In is implemented by inbound mechanisms (Chapter 2); Request-Reply by a synchronous callout; Batch Data Synchronization by Batch Apex plus Scheduled Apex; and UI Update Based on Data Changes by Platform Events or CDC driving a live component.

questions.prompt: Per Salesforce's Pattern Selection Guide as taught in this course, what is the first question asked when choosing an integration pattern, and why is it asked before sync-vs-async?
options: Is this about a process (an action happening) or data (records syncing)? — asked first because sync-vs-async alone can't distinguish Request-Reply from UI Update Based on Data Changes, since both can involve asynchronous elements
Does the external system use JSON or XML? — asked first because format determines every later decision
How many callouts will this require? — asked first to avoid exceeding governor limits
Is a Named Credential already configured? — asked first since nothing else can proceed without one
questions.explain: The process-vs-data question is asked first specifically because sync-vs-async by itself doesn't cleanly separate an action-oriented requirement (Request-Reply/Fire and Forget) from a data-syncing one (Batch Sync/UI Update), both of which can have asynchronous elements.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Order Sync practice project's architecture in the correct order.
items: An after-update trigger on Order__c detects a transition to Status = 'Submitted' and enqueues a Queueable job
The Queueable job's execute() method makes the HTTP callout to the external order system first
The Queueable job performs the DML update to Order__c's Fulfillment_Status__c field
If the callout fails, the job re-enqueues itself with an incremented attempt counter, up to a capped number of attempts
questions.explain: The trigger enqueues the Queueable rather than calling out directly (since its own transaction has pending DML); inside the Queueable's own fresh transaction, the callout happens first, then the DML update, correctly honoring the transaction-ordering rule; and a failure triggers the capped retry pattern from Lesson 6.

questions.prompt: In the Address Validation practice project, why can't a before-save Apex trigger or before-save Flow make the validation callout directly?
options: Because a before-save context already has DML pending as part of that very save, and a callout can't run while DML is pending in the same transaction
Because before-save triggers cannot read field values
Because address-validation APIs never accept JSON
Because before-save Flows automatically disable all callouts platform-wide
questions.explain: This is the same transaction-ordering rule from Chapter 1 applied to a before-save context — the pending DML of that very save blocks any callout, which is why the project needs either a Screen Flow (before any save occurs) or an after-insert async follow-up instead.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the three-layer approach to monitoring an integration taught in this course's final lesson.
options: Custom logging (like a failure record on an attempt-capped retry job) captures errors the code's own try/catch already handled, which the default exception email would not
The built-in unhandled-exception email is a backstop for anything that slips past the code's own error handling entirely
Event Monitoring's Apex Unexpected Exception event type gives a durable, queryable record of unhandled exceptions over time
Relying on the unhandled-exception email alone is Salesforce's own recommended monitoring strategy
Querying EventLogFile requires the View Event Log Files and API Enabled permissions
questions.explain: Custom logging catches errors already handled by try/catch; the exception email backstops fully unhandled failures; Event Monitoring gives durable, queryable trend data; and EventLogFile access requires both named permissions. Salesforce's own documentation explicitly discourages relying only on the exception email as a monitoring strategy — the opposite of that last statement.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Event Monitoring event type that records unhandled Apex exceptions in structured Event Log Files is called Apex ________ Exception.
questions.explain: The "Apex Unexpected Exception" event type is Event Monitoring's structured, queryable record of unhandled exceptions, distinct from the default one-off notification email.

questions.prompt: A business has both an interactive web form where customers enter their address and a bulk nightly import that creates Contacts with no user present. Which approach to address validation from this course's practice project fits best?
options: Both: a Screen Flow HTTP Callout for the interactive form, and an after-insert trigger enqueuing an async Queueable validation job as a safety net for the bulk import path
Only a before-save Apex trigger, since it covers every creation path uniformly
Only the Screen Flow approach, since bulk-imported Contacts never need validation
Only the asynchronous after-insert approach, since interactive users don't benefit from immediate feedback
questions.explain: The interactive path benefits from immediate feedback during entry (Screen Flow callout, before any save occurs), while the non-interactive bulk-import path has no user present to watch a screen and needs the after-insert async safety net instead — many real systems need both to cover every creation path.
